tip: Two spends: time is passed – 'paso mucho tiempo' – money is spent ('gastar'). 'Gastar tiempo' sounds like wasting it.
Both verbs share this sentence: 'es normal' states a general truth, so 'ser'; 'estar nervioso' marks a temporary state – the nerves will pass, so 'estar'.
Why 'ayude', not 'ayudo'? After 'quieres que', the helping is only wished-for, not yet real – Spanish marks unreal events with the subjunctive's flipped -e ending.
No apostrophe-s exists: 'los padres de mi novio' = the parents OF my boyfriend. Flip English possessives around 'de' – the owner comes last.
'Los días' – 'día' ends in -a yet is masculine, alongside 'el mapa' and 'el problema'. A small club of -a masculines everyone trips on once.
Built like 'gustar': the real subject is 'ver a sus nietos' – the seeing makes 'ilusión', and 'le' just marks who receives the thrill. The excited person is never the subject.
'Jugar' demands 'a': 'juega AL fútbol' – literally plays TO the soccer, article included. Bare 'jugar fútbol' sounds off in Spain.
'Tres veces al día' – literally 'to the day'. Spanish rates lean on 'al' / 'a la': 'al día', 'a la semana', where English says per.
'No dice nada' – two negatives, and that's the correct form. Spanish demands the double: 'no' before the verb, 'nada' after. Bare 'dice nada' is broken.
That 'se' changes the verb: 'dormir' = to sleep, 'dormirse' = to FALL asleep. 'Se duerme en el carro' – she drifts off, not just sleeps.
'Encantada' ends in -a because María is the one speaking – this 'delighted' agrees with the speaker's own gender. A man introducing himself says 'encantado'.
After a superlative, English 'in' turns into 'de': 'la más puntual del equipo' – of the team. 'En el equipo' is the instinct; 'de' is the rule.
By train = 'en tren' – bare noun, no article: 'en tren', 'en avión', 'en autobús'. Walking is the odd one out: 'a pie'.
Spanish dates use plain numbers – 'el dos', 'el quince' – with one exception: the 1st. 'El primero' is the only ordinal used on the calendar, exactly as in this sentence.
A place, yet 'sé' not 'conozco': where the station is counts as a fact, and facts belong to 'saber'. 'Conocer la estación' would mean you've actually been there.
'Pide helado' – 'pedir' already means ask FOR, so no extra word. 'Preguntar' is only for asking questions. Spanish splits 'ask' in two.
'Cruza' looks exactly like 'he/she crosses' – because it is that form. Affirmative 'tú' commands borrow the 'él/ella' present; only the missing subject tells you it's an order.
'Ser' + 'de' expresses origin. 'Soy de España' = I'm from Spain. Use 'vivir en' for where you live now.
'Es viudo' takes 'ser': marital status defines identity, not a passing state.
'Hace + time + que + present tense' expresses duration: 'Hace un cuarto de hora que te espero' = I've been waiting for you for fifteen minutes.
'¿Tienes hijos?' keeps statement word order – Spanish yes/no questions often do; intonation does the work.
Steak doneness: 'poco hecho' (barely done) = rare, 'al punto' (at the point) = medium, 'bien hecho' = well done – the standard terms waiters use.
'Estoy' is 'estar' – used for temporary states, like how you feel right now.
'Usted' – formal you, used in service contexts and with strangers.
'Está lista' = dinner's ready, but 'es lista' = she's smart. With some adjectives, 'ser' vs 'estar' changes the meaning, not just the timing.
'Somos' alone already says 'we are' – so why 'nosotros'? Spanish drops subject pronouns, and keeping one adds weight: WE are from Spain, whatever the rest of you are.
Missing someone? 'Extraño' is the Latin American verb; in Spain you'd hear 'echo de menos a mi familia.' Same feeling, different phrase – pick your side of the Atlantic.
'Estar' for location: 'Está en Madrid.' Physical position always uses 'estar' (except events).
'Estar' for taste/experience: 'La sopa está rica.' How something tastes/seems right now → 'estar'.
'Estar' for resulting states: 'Está roto.' The door isn't broken by nature – it became broken. Result of change → 'estar'.
